tip: 'Le' shrinks before a vowel: 'le après-midi' becomes 'l'après-midi', the 'e' dropped and joined on.
Two past tenses in one breath: 'connaissais' is the ongoing state (already knew), 'a posé' the single action that happened.
'Jaloux' (masculine) becomes 'jalouse' (feminine). Adjectives ending in '-oux' usually change to '-ouse' in the feminine – 'doux' is an exception ('douce').
'Mignon' (masculine) becomes 'mignonne' (feminine). Adjectives ending in '-on' double the 'n' in the feminine: 'bon' becomes 'bonne'.
'Mou' means soft or squishy: 'le canapé est mou'. It's an oddball – its feminine is 'molle', not 'moue'.
To say what day it is, French uses 'we are': 'nous sommes lundi' = it's Monday, literally 'we are Monday'.
'Tout va bien' is literally 'everything goes well' – French checks how things are with 'aller' (to go), not 'être' (to be). The same verb hides in 'comment ça va ?'.
French makes grooming verbs reflexive: 'elle se maquille' is literally 'she makes herself up'. The 'se' points the action back on her – no English 'herself' needed.
'Pour emporter' = to go / takeaway. 'Sur place' = to eat in. Common at restaurants and cafés.
'Ça ne fait rien' is literally 'that does nothing' = no worries / it doesn't matter. The 'ne ... rien' pair wraps the verb to mean 'nothing'.
'Avoir horreur de' = to hate/detest something. An 'avoir' expression: 'j'ai horreur du lundi' = I hate Mondays.
'Salut' is informal for both 'hi' and 'bye'. 'Ça va ?' is a casual way to ask 'how are you?'
Like English 'going to', French uses 'aller' + verb for the near future: 'je vais ... partir' = I'm going to leave.
'Ça fait longtemps' = it's been a while. 'Ça fait' + a length of time expresses duration: 'ça fait deux ans' = it's been two years.
'Il y a' means 'there is', not 'he has' (that's 'il a'). The 'y' is mandatory: 'il y a du soleil' = it's sunny.
'Qu'est-ce qui' asks 'what' as the subject, the thing doing the action: 'qu'est-ce qui s'est passé' = what happened. Use 'qu'est-ce que' when 'what' is the object.
Dates use plain numbers where English counts 'fifteenth': 'le quinze mars'. Only the 1st is different – 'le premier' (the first).
'Partir' uses 'être' in the past: 'elle est partie'. The past form 'partie' adds an 'e' to match the feminine subject.
French doesn't 'agree' with a verb – you are in agreement: 'être d'accord'. 'Je suis d'accord' = literally 'I am of agreement'.
'Dix-huit heures' = 18:00. France runs on the 24-hour clock for schedules, so 6pm becomes eighteen hundred: 'dix-huit heures', not 'six heures'.
'Des' normally shrinks to 'de' when an adjective comes before the noun: 'de nouvelles recettes', not 'des nouvelles recettes'.
'Profiter de' means to make the most of, not just profit: 'nous avons profité du beau temps' = we enjoyed the nice weather.
You climb into a vehicle in French – 'monter dans': 'elle est montée dans le taxi' = she got into the taxi.
'Il y a' = there is / there are. Works for both singular and plural. 'Il y a du monde' = there are people / it's crowded.
'Cinq heures moins le quart' is 'five hours minus the quarter' = 4:45. Before the hour French subtracts: 'moins le quart' = quarter to.
Homework is always plural in French: 'mes devoirs'. 'Le devoir' on its own means duty – the plural shifts it to schoolwork.
'Nouveau' turns into 'nouvel' before a vowel sound, for smoothness: 'un nouvel appartement', not 'un nouveau appartement'.
'Eu', the past form of 'avoir', is pronounced just like the letter 'u' – the 'e' is silent: 'nous avons eu' = we had.
'Arrête de' + a verb = stop doing something. 'Commence à' + a verb = start doing something.
'Changer de' takes no 'le' or 'un': 'elle a changé de travail' = she changed jobs. It's 'changed of job', same with 'changer de train'.
